newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Private investment alone can't solve poverty - U.N..
newsitem.headline: Private investment alone can't solve poverty - U.N..

text.p: With more than 1.3 billion people living in extreme poverty, a senior U.N. official said that poor nations could not depend on private investment alone to lift up their economies.

Inaugurating the International Year for the Eradication of Poverty, James Gustave Speth, head of U.N. Development Programme, said on Thursday that people forgot about foreign assistance to nations in southeast Asia, like Malaysia, now experiencing prosperity.
"We too often forget that behind the Asian miracle was a long period of development cooperation," he told a news conference.

Speth, an American, said that official government aid had fallen 25 percent in the last four years while private investment increased. But he said that 80 percent of such investment to developing nations was directed to 12 medium-income countries, adding: "There is no correlation between direct foreign investment and real need."
He maintained that the world had the money and skills to eradicate poverty but lacked the political will.
"We have the resources, the know-how. We just need the momentum, the political support and the financial support to do it," he said.

In the United States, once the world's largest aid donor, foreign aid has dropped 40 percent in real terms since 1985, according to U.S. statistics. Washington now provides less than 20 percent of the world's foreign assistance.

According to U.N. documents one out of every five people in the world suffers from debilitating poverty, which means a lack of material resources as well as control over land, skills, knowledge, capital and social connections.

The gap between rich and poor is widening both within countries and between developed and developing nations. The income ratio between the richest 20 percent and the poorest 20 percent was 30:1 in 1960; it had increased to 61:1 by 1991.

The largest concentration of severely impoverished people live in southern Asia -- India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Maldives, Sri Lanka, Bhutan and Nepal. And among industrial countries in Western Europe and the United States, 15 percent of the population live below national poverty lines.
"The goal to eradicate extreme poverty," Speth said, "is not some lofty idealism when we see how many industrial countries over the course of this century have done just that."
